questions.q: A wire 0.50 m long carries a current of 3.0 A at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density 0.20 T. What is the force on the wire?
questions.solution: With the current perpendicular to the field: \(F = BIl\) = 0.20 × 3.0 × 0.50 = 0.30 N.

questions.q: In Fleming's left-hand rule, what do the thumb, first finger and second finger represent, in that order?
questions.solution: The thumb gives the direction of the force (motion), the first finger the field, and the second finger the conventional current. The three are at right angles to each other. For a moving electron, the current is opposite to its velocity.

questions.q: Which is the correct definition of the tesla?

options.A: The flux density that gives a force of one newton on a charge of one coulomb.
options.B: The flux through an area of one square metre.
options.C: The flux density that gives a force of one newton on each metre of a wire carrying one ampere at right angles to the field.
options.D: The flux density that induces one volt in a coil of one turn.

questions.solution: Flux density is defined from \(F = BIl\): one tesla is the flux density that produces a force of one newton per metre on a wire carrying a current of one ampere perpendicular to the field.

questions.q: An electron moves at \(2.0 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\) at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density 0.10 T. What is the force on it? (\(e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}\))

An electron moves at \(2.0 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\) at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density \(1.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{T}\). What is the radius of its path? (\(e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}\), \(m_{e} = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\ \text{kg}\))
questions.solution: The magnetic force provides the centripetal force: \(BQv = \frac{mv^{2}}{r}\). So \(r = \frac{mv}{BQ} = \frac{9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 2.0 \times 10^{6}}{1.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19}} = 1.1 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{m}\).

questions.q: Why does a magnetic field not change the speed of a charged particle moving through it?

options.A: The magnetic force is too small.
options.B: The magnetic force acts along the direction of motion.
options.C: The magnetic force acts only on stationary charges.
options.D: The magnetic force is always at right angles to the velocity, so it does no work.

questions.solution: The force on a moving charge is perpendicular to both the field and the velocity. A force at right angles to the motion does no work, so the kinetic energy and speed stay constant. Only the direction changes, which is why the path is a circle.

questions.q: A magnetic field of flux density 0.50 T passes at right angles through an area of \(0.020\ \text{m}^{2}\). What is the magnetic flux through the area?
questions.solution: With the field perpendicular to the area: \(\Phi = BA\) = 0.50 × 0.020 = 0.010 Wb.

questions.q: A coil of 200 turns and area \(5.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^{2}\) lies with its plane at right angles to a field of flux density 0.10 T. What is the flux linkage?
questions.solution: Flux linkage is the flux through one turn multiplied by the number of turns: \(N\Phi = BAN = 0.10 \times 5.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 200 = 0.10\ \text{Wb turns}\). Leaving out the number of turns gives the flux through one turn.

questions.q: What does Faraday's law say about the e.m.f. induced in a coil?

options.A: It is proportional to the flux linkage.
options.B: It is proportional to the resistance of the coil.
options.C: It is proportional to the flux density.
options.D: It is proportional to the rate of change of flux linkage.

questions.solution: Faraday's law: the size of the induced e.m.f. is proportional to the rate of change of flux linkage, \(\varepsilon = N\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}\). A steady flux, however large, induces nothing.

questions.q: The flux linkage of a coil falls steadily from 0.60 Wb turns to 0.20 Wb turns in 0.050 s. What is the size of the induced e.m.f.?
questions.solution: The change in flux linkage is 0.60 − 0.20 = 0.40 Wb turns. Induced e.m.f. = change in flux linkage ÷ time = 0.40 ÷ 0.050 = 8.0 V. Use the change, not the starting value.

questions.q: What does Lenz's law say about the direction of an induced current?

options.A: It is in the direction that opposes the change that causes it.
options.B: It is in the direction that increases the change that causes it.
options.D: It is always in the same direction as the magnetic field.

questions.solution: An induced current flows in the direction that opposes the change producing it. This follows from conservation of energy: if it helped the change along, energy would appear from nowhere.

questions.q: A magnet dropped through a vertical copper tube falls much more slowly than through a plastic tube. Why?

options.A: Copper is magnetic and attracts the magnet.
options.B: Air resistance is greater in the copper tube.
options.D: Currents induced in the copper produce a magnetic field that opposes the motion of the magnet.

questions.solution: The moving magnet changes the flux through the copper, inducing currents in it. By Lenz's law these currents set up a field that opposes the magnet's motion, giving an upward force. Plastic does not conduct, so no currents flow. Copper itself is not magnetic.

questions.q: An alternating supply has a peak voltage of 325 V. What is its root mean square voltage?
questions.solution: \(V_{rms} = \frac{V_{0}}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{325}{\sqrt{2}}\) = 230 V. This is the steady voltage that would deliver the same power, and it is the value quoted for the mains.

questions.q: An ideal transformer has 1000 turns on its primary coil and 100 turns on its secondary coil. The primary is connected to a 230 V alternating supply. What is the secondary voltage?
questions.solution: \(\frac{V_{s}}{V_{p}} = \frac{N_{s}}{N_{p}}\), so the secondary voltage = 230 × 100 ÷ 1000 = 23 V. Fewer turns on the secondary means a step-down transformer.

questions.q: Why is the core of a transformer made of thin laminated sheets, not a solid block of iron?

options.B: To increase the resistance of the coils.
options.C: To reduce the eddy currents induced in the core.
options.D: To stop the core becoming magnetised.

questions.solution: The changing flux induces currents in the iron core itself, called eddy currents, which heat it and waste energy. Thin sheets insulated from each other break up the paths these currents can take, so they are much smaller.

questions.q: Why is electrical power transmitted across the country at very high voltage?

options.A: For a given power the current is smaller, so less energy is wasted heating the cables.
options.B: High voltage makes the current travel faster.
options.C: High voltage is safer than low voltage.
options.D: For a given power the current is larger, so more energy arrives.

questions.solution: \(P = IV\), so sending the same power at a higher voltage needs a smaller current. The power wasted in the cables is \(I^{2}R\), so a smaller current cuts the loss sharply. Transformers step the voltage up for transmission and down again for use.
